svg.aria-label: A 3,008-byte ping cut into three fragments by the Pi, and the reply's fragments cut again into five by a smaller link

g.text: 3,008 bytes of ICMP: too big for one 1,500-byte frame
reassembled at the Pi: 3,008 bytes, checksum ✓

ol.li: The Pi pings 1.1.1.1 with 3,000 bytes of data. With the 8-byte ping header, that’s 3,008 bytes: far too big for one Ethernet frame, whose limit is 1,500 bytes including the 20-byte IP header.

So the Pi cuts it into fragments. Each gets its own IP header, with the same identification number, the “more fragments” flag on all but the last, and an offset saying where its data belongs. The offset counts in units of 8 bytes, so every piece but the last holds a multiple of 8.

The reply comes back from 1.1.1.1 in three pieces too, but somewhere on the way, a link with a limit of 1,492 bytes (the PPPoE connection from Chapter 18) can’t fit the two big ones. A router there cuts each of them in two: 1,472 bytes, and a tiny 8-byte leftover. Five fragments arrive.
Only the final destination glues the pieces together, using the offsets, in whatever order they arrive. If even one piece is lost, the whole packet is thrown away after a timeout.

figure.figcaption: Real fragments, from a real ping: ping -s 3000 1.1.1.1 on the Pi.
